title: Lincoln did not scribble it on an envelope.
description:
Lincoln did not scribble it on an envelope. The tale of a hurried draft on the back of an envelope, written on the train, was popularised by Mary Raymond Shipman Andrews in her 1906 book The Perfect Tribute.

The drafts look calm. The National Constitution Center argues against the train story because the draft copies are in Lincoln's normal, steady handwriting.

Nobody knows exactly where. Historians are divided over whether he wrote it in the weeks before, on the train, or the evening before at David Wills' house. He began work soon after the July 1863 battle.

Lincoln wrote out five known manuscript copies: Nicolay, Hay, Everett, Bancroft and Bliss. Only the Bliss copy bears his signature.

Edward Everett spoke for two hours. Lincoln followed with brief dedicatory remarks. Everett is quoted as saying he came as near to the central idea in two hours as Lincoln did in two minutes.

A better story is not a better source.

Established that the envelope story is called perhaps the biggest myth about the address, that Lincoln started work soon after the July 1863 battle, that the drafts are in his normal steady handwriting, that Everett spoke for about two hours, and Everett's two hours versus two minutes remark.
